findings.nist_csf: PR.IP-1 / PR.DS-5 (Secure config / data leak protection)
findings.description: The Spring Boot Actuator (env) endpoint at /actuator/env is publicly reachable and returned its expected content. findings.title: CRLF injection / HTTP response splitting in 'url'
findings.nist_csf: PR.IP-1 / PR.DS-5 (Secure config / data leak protection)
findings.description: A CRLF sequence injected via 'url' produced an attacker-controlled response header (a sentinel header and Set-Cookie appeared in the response). This HTTP response splitting enables session fixation, cache poisoning, and reflected XSS by smuggling headers or a second response body.
findings.remediation: Strip or reject CR (%0d) and LF (%0a) in any user input copied into response headers (Location, Set-Cookie, etc.); use the framework's header API, which rejects embedded newlines, rather than string concatenation.

evidence.notes: injected header/cookie reflected in the response header block

findings.title: Web cache deception: dynamic page served at a static URL (/account/orthrus-wcd-f3d751.css)

findings.description: Appending '/<file>.css' to /account returned the original dynamic page verbatim instead of a 404. A CDN or proxy that caches by file extension can then store this 'static' response and serve one user's private content to others. The response carries cache indicators.
findings.remediation: Make the origin return 404 for unknown sub-paths of dynamic routes; configure the cache to key on the full normalized path and never cache responses that set cookies or vary by session, regardless of the URL's apparent extension.

findings.remediation: Do not reflect unkeyed request headers into responses; include all influential headers in the cache key, or strip X-Forwarded-* at the edge.

findings.title: GraphQL query batching enabled
findings.nist_csf: PR.IP-1 / PR.DS-5 (Secure config / data leak protection)
findings.description: The endpoint accepted a JSON array of operations and returned an array of results. Batching lets an attacker pack many operations into one request - amplifying rate-limited actions (e.g. login/OTP brute-force) and resource use.
findings.remediation: Disable query batching, or enforce a per-request operation cap and apply rate limiting against the aggregate, not per HTTP request.

findings.title: GraphQL alias overloading (no query-cost limit)
findings.nist_csf: PR.IP-1 / PR.DS-5 (Secure config / data leak protection)
findings.description: The endpoint resolved all 100 aliases of a single field in one request with no cost/complexity limit. An attacker can multiply server work arbitrarily within one query - an alias-amplification DoS primitive.
findings.remediation: Enforce query cost analysis / complexity limits and cap the number of aliased fields per request (e.g. graphql-query-complexity, depth limits).

findings.title: GraphQL accepts circular fragments (recursion DoS)
findings.nist_csf: PR.IP-1 / PR.DS-5 (Secure config / data leak protection)
findings.description: The endpoint executed a query containing a circular fragment spread instead of rejecting it with a validation error. Fragment cycles that a server fails to reject can be amplified into a recursion / resource-exhaustion denial of service.
findings.remediation: Use a spec-compliant GraphQL implementation that rejects fragment cycles, and enforce query depth / complexity limits.

findings.title: Host header injection (attacker-controlled host reflected into links/redirects)
findings.nist_csf: PR.IP-1 / PR.DS-5 (Secure config / data leak protection)
findings.description: A sentinel host sent in the 'Host'/'X-Forwarded-Host' request header was reflected back into an absolute URL in the body. When the application builds absolute URLs (password-reset and email-confirmation links, redirects, or script/link src) from the incoming host header, an attacker can set it to a domain they control. A victim who clicks the resulting link - e.g. a poisoned password-reset email - leaks the secret token to the attacker (account takeover); the same primitive enables web-cache poisoning and, where the host selects an upstream, SSRF.
findings.remediation: Do not trust the incoming Host or X-Forwarded-* headers to build absolute URLs or routing decisions. Validate Host against an allow-list of expected hostnames (reject mismatches with 400), build links from a server-side canonical base URL, and strip X-Forwarded-* at the trust boundary.

evidence.notes: forged host reflected into an absolute URL in the body

findings.title: HTTP parameter pollution: duplicate 'q' silently dropped
findings.nist_csf: PR.IP-1 / PR.DS-5 (Secure config / data leak protection)
findings.description: Sending 'q' twice in one query string caused the server to keep only the first occurrence and discard the other. When a security control (WAF rule, authorization filter, or input validator) inspects the discarded copy while application code reads the surviving one, an attacker can smuggle a malicious value past the control via the dropped duplicate.
findings.remediation: Reject requests containing duplicate parameter keys, or normalize them consistently across every layer (proxy, WAF, framework, application) so no component disagrees about which value is authoritative.

evidence.notes: server kept the first duplicate (sentinel orthrushpp28f58ca)

top_findings.title: OS command injection in GraphQL argument 'systemDiagnostics.cmd'
top_findings.nist_csf: PR.IP-1 / PR.DS-5 (Secure config / data leak protection)
top_findings.description: A shell metacharacter + canary injected into the GraphQL argument 'cmd' of 'mutation systemDiagnostics' was executed - the canary was echoed back by the OS shell, proving arbitrary command execution via a GraphQL resolver.
top_findings.remediation: Never pass GraphQL argument values to a shell; use argument-vector process APIs with a fixed command and strict allow-listing of inputs.

top_findings.title: Unrestricted file upload (.php accepted) at /upload
top_findings.nist_csf: PR.IP-1 / PR.DS-5 (Secure config / data leak protection)
top_findings.description: The upload endpoint /upload accepted a file with a dangerous '.php' extension. If uploaded files are served from the web root or interpreted by the server, an attacker can upload a web shell (RCE) or a .svg/.html for stored XSS. The probe uploaded a harmless inert marker, not a working payload - confirm where the file lands and whether it executes.
top_findings.remediation: Validate uploads by content (magic bytes) and an allow-list of extensions/MIME types; store outside the web root with a generated name; serve via a handler that forces a non-executable Content-Type and Content-Disposition: attachment.

top_findings.title: LLM prompt injection via 'message' (instructions overridden)
top_findings.nist_csf: PR.IP-1 / PR.DS-5 (Secure config / data leak protection)
top_findings.description: An injected instruction sent through 'message' caused the model to ignore its system/developer prompt and emit an attacker-chosen canary token verbatim (OWASP LLM01). An attacker can hijack the model to exfiltrate data, call tools/functions, produce harmful output, or bypass guardrails.
top_findings.remediation: Treat all model output as untrusted; separate system and user content with a robust template, constrain tool/function calls with allow-lists and human review, apply input/output filtering, and never let model output drive privileged actions without authorization checks.
